candidate.answerReason: Enforcing positivity of every logarithm argument gives the domain (1/256,1/16). Its length is 15/256 in lowest terms, so m+n=271.

methods.label: Work inward from the outer logarithm
methods.explanation:
Every logarithm must have a positive argument. Starting with the outermost logarithm lets us translate that requirement inward, one layer at a time.

Write
\[
t=\log_{1/16}x,\qquad u=\log_{16}t,
\]
\[
v=\log_{1/4}u,\qquad w=\log_4v.
\]
Then \(f(x)=\log_{1/2}w\), so we need \(w>0\). Because base \(4\) is greater than \(1\), this means \(v>1\). Next, base \(1/4\) is between \(0\) and \(1\), so its logarithm is decreasing. Including the positive-argument condition, we obtain
\[
v>1\iff 0<u<\frac14.
\]
Since base \(16\) is greater than \(1\),
\[
0<\log_{16}t<\frac14
\iff 1<t<16^{1/4}=2.
\]
Finally, base \(1/16\) is less than \(1\), so the inequalities reverse when we return to \(x\):
\[
1<\log_{1/16}x<2
\iff \frac1{256}<x<\frac1{16}.
\]
These steps are reversible, and this last interval makes every intermediate logarithm well defined with the required positive argument. Both endpoints are excluded because the conditions are strict.

The interval length is
\[
\frac1{16}-\frac1{256}=\frac{15}{256}.
\]
The numerator and denominator are relatively prime, so \(m+n=15+256=\boxed{271}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
